title: A hundred times a day
hookLine: balihaaree gur aapne: I'm a sacrifice to my Guru a hundred times a day, who made angels of men (Asa di Var, ang 462)

lines: A TEACHER WHO CHANGED A LIFE.
cards: Ask people about a teacher who changed their life, and watch their faces. A high school English teacher who said, you can write. A coach who saw something before anyone else did.
A grandmother who taught them to pray, or to cook, or to forgive. Plenty of those teachers never heard a real thank-you, or heard it once, years too late.
Guru Nanak opens his great ballad not with God's power, not with a warning, but with a thank-you to the Guru, said a hundred times a day.

teach.h: BALIHAAREE: I'D GIVE MYSELF FOR YOU.
teach.b: The first salok of Asa di Var, in paraphrase: I am a sacrifice to my Guru a hundred times a day, who made angels out of human beings, and took no time to do it. Balihaaree is the first word.
It means I am a sacrifice to you, I'd give myself for you: the language of overflowing love and gratitude, the kind a mother might whisper over a child.
Diuhaarree sad vaar: in a day, a hundred times. Not once, at a graduation. Over and over, every day.

Maanas te devte: from humans, devtas, angels or godlike beings. The Guru's teaching takes ordinary, struggling people and makes them shine. And karat na laagee vaar: in the doing of it, there was no delay.
Listen to that last word, vaar. Here it means delay.
Just before, sad vaar meant a hundred times. And the whole bani is a var, a ballad. Some listeners hear a play on that sound in the very first salok.

Who is the Guru here? For Guru Nanak, the true Guru is ultimately God, the Word that teaches from within; Sikhs also honor the human Gurus who carried that Word, and today the Guru Granth Sahib itself.
The salok doesn't separate them. It overflows with thanks.

And there's an idea folded in: the salok doesn't picture people climbing to the angels by sheer effort. It pictures a teacher who lifts. The first emotion of Asa di Var, before any argument, is gratitude for being lifted.

how: Asa di Var opens with Guru Nanak's salok of gratitude to the Guru, balihaaree, a hundred times a day, sung in gurdwaras each morning.

o: a prayer asking forgiveness for sins
I am a sacrifice to you, in deep thanks
an offering of food left at a shrine

s: Asa di Var's first salok is a warning about sin
it's an overflowing thank-you to the Guru.
the salok says the Guru made angels out of human beings
maanas te devte, and without delay.
in this salok, people climb to the angels by effort alone
the salok pictures a Guru who lifts them.

games.q: you're opening a great ballad about God. what does Guru Nanak put first?
o: gratitude to the Guru, a hundred times a day.
games.why: the very first salok is balihaaree: I'm a sacrifice to my Guru a hundred times a day. thanks before any argument.

practice: Let one teacher come to mind, a schoolteacher, a parent, a mentor, an author, someone who lifted you, and picture their face and one specific thing they gave you.
Then thank them silently, as fully as you can, and again if it rises; if you pray, thank the Guru, or God, as the teacher behind all teachers, and say Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Balihaaree, I am a sacrifice to you: Asa di Var's first salok says balihaaree to the Guru a hundred times a day, who made angels of humans without delay.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: balihaaree, I am a sacrifice to you; a word of overflowing love and thanks.

carryVoice: Your line: made angels of men. Gratitude, a hundred times over, every single day. Until tomorrow.
